strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP evaluation problem: repeated stimuli across participants and overlapping fMRI windows can inflate estimates of generalization to unseen subjects and language. Joint subject-and-stimulus holdout is a sensible protocol for that goal.

The experiments cover two modalities, two public datasets, and two established models. Additional held-out evaluation and shuffled-input controls are useful diagnostics, and the reported performance gaps warrant careful investigation.

Appendix E explicitly examines generation without teacher forcing. Table 6 retains differences between splitting methods, providing some evidence that the observed effects extend beyond teacher-forced evaluation. The paper also acknowledges the data-discarding cost of its proposed protocol.
weaknesses: The proposed benchmark still uses teacher-forced evaluation. Table 6 identifies the main results, including Table 5, as using teacher forcing during generation. Supplying ground-truth prefixes can sustain performance with shuffled brain signals, so Table 4 does not isolate memorization caused by split contamination. The free-generation results in Table 6 are valuable, but the additional-test and shuffled-input controls also need to be repeated without test-time target prefixes, and the benchmark should use that setting.

The published pseudocode does not enforce the claimed absence of leakage. Algorithm 1, line 15, excludes held-out subjects but permits training edges connected to held-out texts; Algorithm 2, line 33, excludes held-out stories but permits held-out subjects. These expansion rules contradict the joint restrictions in Equations 13–14. This could be a transcription problem, but the manuscript does not establish which implementation produced the experimental splits.

The formal analysis contains substantive errors. Equations 6–7 require every training example to have a corresponding subject or text in the test set, although partial overlap already constitutes leakage under the paper's definition. Equation 17 measures exact signal overlap rather than shared subject identity and leaves zero training denominators unspecified. Appendix D's claim that discarding samples is always necessary also assumes connectivity not guaranteed by the dataset definition; disconnected subject–stimulus components provide a counterexample.

Reported evaluation metrics are internally inconsistent. Table 5 gives EEG2Text ROUGE precision 23.95, recall 23.98, and F1 25.74, which is incompatible with standard F1 computation under consistent aggregation. Table 7 labels 40.65 as recall for Narratives method (a), whereas Tables 3–4 label that value as F1. These discrepancies require an audit of the evaluation code and corrected tables before the benchmark can be trusted.

The evidence does not establish the claimed encoder degradation. Decreasing validation reconstruction loss in Figure 5 does not demonstrate worsening representations on unseen subjects. Likewise, improving test performance with longer training is not sufficient evidence of leakage. The supplementary fMRI comparison additionally changes encoder initialization and learning rate, preventing a clean attribution to training duration or contamination.

The universal claim that existing splitting methods are 'wrong' exceeds the demonstrated scope. Evaluation on new subjects with familiar stimuli and evaluation on familiar subjects with new stimuli answer legitimate, distinct questions. Joint holdout is appropriate for simultaneous generalization along both axes; the paper should distinguish that target from other evaluation settings and substantiate its criticism of prior work against their stated claims.

Reproducibility and experimental attribution remain insufficient. The manuscript supplies some hyperparameters, but no code or split-manifest link, retained/discarded sample counts, precise construction of the additional test set, or clear shuffling granularity. Four-seed uncertainty is reported only for leakage rates, not decoding results. An identical nominal 80:10:10 ratio does not control training-set size or test difficulty after discarding data. Corrected implementations, documented splits, and controlled free-generation evaluations are needed before this contribution meets the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings.
